results.summary: This design uses combinational logic gates to decode dip switch settings into segment patterns for a seven-segment display. It is configured by setting the eight DIP switches, which select which segments to illuminate. The project requires an external LED display to show the segments. The documentation is minimal and does not provide a clear mapping of switch settings to segments, so the exact behavior is not fully specified.

This design implements a simple AND gate logic function, with outputs labeled as 't1 and' and 't1 and 2'. It is intended to be run as-is, with no specific test procedure described. The external hardware requirement is unspecified, with the documentation stating it can be anything. The documentation is extremely thin, providing almost no detail about the design's purpose or operation.

This design prints names (boris, dario, ivan, natasa) on a seven-segment display, with a period used as a separator. It is intended for a Tiny Tapeout workshop at Supercon 25, but the testing procedure and external hardware are not yet documented. The design operates at a low clock speed of 2 Hz. The documentation is incomplete, with placeholders for testing and hardware details.

This project is described as having something to do with Meshtastic, but the documentation explicitly states that the author does not yet know what it will do. The pins are generically named as inputs and outputs, with no functional description. The external hardware is suggested to be a T-Echo, but this is uncertain. The documentation is essentially non-existent, providing no useful information about the design.

This design converts a 4-bit binary input (0-9) into signals for a seven-segment display, driving segments A through G and the decimal point. It is tested by applying any binary number from 0 to 9 on the inputs. The project requires an external seven-segment display to show the decoded digits. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic function.

This design consists of 128 daisy-chained D flip-flops, with a single input and output, and several switches. The documentation describes the implementation as 'magic mixed with stuff' and the test procedure as doing 'all the right things in the right places and the right time', which is not informative. It requires two 'encabultors' (likely a misspelling of encabulators) as external hardware, but this is unclear. The documentation is too vague to determine the actual functionality or how to use it.

This design implements a programmable logic function using a 4-input lookup table (LUT). The LUT is configured by presenting a truth table on inputs 4-7, and the function is evaluated with inputs on pins 0 and 1, producing the result on output 0. It requires no external hardware. The documentation is clear and sufficient to understand and test the design.

This design displays the letter 'J' on a seven-segment display when dip switch 1 is active. It is tested by activating dip switch 1, and it requires an external LED display. The documentation is minimal, providing only a basic description of the function and test procedure.

This design implements a JK flip-flop using basic logic gates. The clock is connected to input 1, J to input 0, and K to input 2, with outputs Q and Q-not on outputs 0 and 1. It is tested by applying appropriate signals to the inputs and observing the outputs. No external hardware is required. The documentation is brief but sufficient for a basic understanding.

This design converts a 3-bit binary input (0-7) into decimal digits displayed on a seven-segment display. It is tested by toggling the input switches B2, B1, B0 to select a binary number and observing the corresponding decimal digit on the output segments. The project requires an external seven-segment display. The documentation is clear and includes a truth table approach, making it suitable for educational purposes.
